answer: BM25 ranks documents with a saturated term-frequency score: each query term contributes an IDF weight multiplied by tf*(k1+1)/(tf + k1*(1-b+b*doclen/avgdl)). Its two tuning parameters are k1, which controls term-frequency saturation, and b, which controls length normalization. This fixes tf-idf's unbounded term frequency and poor length handling.

Reciprocal rank fusion merges ranked lists by summing 1/(k+rank) contributions for each document (k=60 typically), so no score normalization is needed — only ranks matter. In hybrid search, the lexical BM25 list and the dense embedding list each catch documents the other misses, and RRF combines them into one ranking using only positions.

Every finite game has a mixed-strategy Nash equilibrium (Nash 1950), but finding one is PPAD-complete (Daskalakis, Goldberg & Papadimitriou 2009), so it may be computationally intractable even though it exists. Dominant-strategy outcomes are rare but computationally clean, which is why mechanism design engineers them.

Forward mode propagates derivatives alongside values using dual numbers and is cheap for few outputs; reverse mode (backpropagation) runs the chain rule backward from a scalar loss so one pass yields gradients for all parameters. Deep learning uses reverse mode because it has millions of parameters but only one scalar loss.

Nyquist-Shannon guarantees exact reconstruction of a bandlimited signal if you sample at more than twice its highest frequency. Sampling below that rate causes aliasing, where high frequencies masquerade as lower ones.

Short reads are broken into overlapping k-mers, nodes are (k−1)-mers, and each k-mer is an edge from its prefix to its suffix. The genome is recovered as an Eulerian path (using every edge once) through the de Bruijn graph, which is efficiently findable — though repeats still limit assembly.

Vickrey (1961) designed the second-price auction: the winner pays the second-highest bid, not their own. Since your bid only decides whether you win and never changes the price you pay, bidding your true value is a dominant strategy.

Dense retrieval solves semantic matching (vocabulary mismatch): it embeds queries and documents into vectors so relevance can be judged by meaning, surfacing relevant documents that share no exact query terms. BM25 is purely lexical - it scores exact term matches over an inverted index, so the trade-off table marks its semantics as "no" where bi-encoder and ColBERT methods score "yes". The wiki calls dense retrieval "the semantic complement to lexical BM25", covering the meaning-based matches that lexical scoring cannot.

In "No Silver Bullet" (1986), Brooks splits software difficulty into essential complexity - inherent in the problem itself, the fashioning of complex conceptual structures that compose the abstract software entity - and accidental complexity, which comes from our tools and the representation of those entities in programming and machine languages and is removable. Past order-of-magnitude gains (high-level languages, time-sharing) worked by removing accidental complexity. Because the essential part is irreducible, Brooks argues no single future advance will give another 10x improvement.

PageRank ranks pages as the stationary distribution of a random surfer who follows links with damping: a page gets high rank when it is likely to be visited at equilibrium, i.e. it is pointed to by many pages or by pages that themselves have high rank. The ranking is computed by power iteration on the sparse web graph - O(edges) per iteration, converging in tens of iterations, which scales to billions of edges.

The open-world assumption means missing information is treated as unknown rather than false: in RDF/OWL a missing triple (for example X marriedTo Y) does not assert they are not married, and the reasoner will not derive negatives you never stated. Databases instead use the closed-world assumption, where not-found equals false, so expecting database-style absence-means-false reasoning gives wrong inferences in description logics.

Analytics queries scan huge tables but usually need only a handful of columns, which they aggregate. Row storage forces reading whole rows, while columnar storage reads 10-100x less data and enables vectorized, cache-friendly execution, which is why Parquet/Arrow, column stores, and lakehouses dominate data engineering.
